summary: This page from the Emotion Typology site defines sensory pleasure as the feeling when something pleases the senses of seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, or touching. It argues the emotion is primordial and likely innate and universal, linked to survival cues, while noting modern pleasures such as abstract art and death metal that seem to contradict those origins. It also describes the behavioral effect of savoring a stimulus and how people schedule time for such experiences.
one_line: Defines sensory pleasure as the positive emotion felt when the senses encounter something pleasant, beautiful, or delightful, and discusses its evolutionary roots.
key_facts: Sensory pleasure is defined as the feeling when something happens that pleases your senses.
You feel sensory pleasure when you see, hear, smell, taste, or touch something that is pleasant, delicious, beautiful or delightful.
Examples given include seeing a beautiful layered cake, getting a full-body massage, and smelling a rose that has just come in flower.
The page describes sensory pleasure as, like its negative counterpart disgust, a primordial emotion.
Things that give sensory pleasure generally help us (or used to help us) survive and thrive, such as identifying nutritious foods like bright-colored fruits.
Examples of survival-linked pleasure include being in protective company, such as sitting on a parent's lap, or being in a safe environment with a wide view of the surroundings.
The page states that sensory pleasure seems innate and universal, with gentle sounds, soft touches, curvy shapes, and calm movements found pleasant from birth.
One-day-old babies already look longer at attractive faces than at less-attractive faces, citing Slater et al. (1998).
People enjoy complex abstract paintings, death metal music, rollercoasters, and funky-smelling cheeses on a direct, visceral level.
Research fields such as aesthetics, philosophy of mind, and evolutionary psychology try to explain how and why people derive pleasure from these things.
The behavioral effect of sensory pleasure is to savor the stimulus and take it in, such as continuing to watch a sunset or pet a soft-coated dog.
Having time to savor is described as an important precondition for having the emotion in the first place.
People plan moments for sensory pleasure, such as free evenings for restaurant meals, Sunday afternoons at museums, and holidays to admire landscapes.
Typical expressions listed are "That smells great." and "Look at that, so beautiful!"
Cited sources include Ekman (2003), 'Sixteen enjoyable emotions' in Emotion Researcher, and Matthen (2014), 'Eye candy' on Aeon.co.
